units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay, you've found it, and you've stepped from a cobbled street into a glass tunnel.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Look up. That's a glass roof, held up by a delicate cast-iron frame, arching over a long shopping street.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: This is the Galeries Royales Saint-Hubert.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: It's gorgeous.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's about two hundred and thirteen meters long, and it opened on the twentieth of June 1847, inaugurated by King Leopold the First and his two sons.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The architect was Jean-Pierre Cluysenaar, who designed and built it between 1846 and 1847.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And it's often described as...

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: One of the first truly public covered shopping arcades in Europe.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Paris had its famous covered passages, but this one was built to be a public street, open to everyone.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Its motto, in Latin, is Omnibus omnia.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Everything for everybody.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: That's the idea. It was a very nineteenth-century dream, a clean, dry, well-lit street where anyone could stroll, shop, and be seen.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And this is three galleries.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Three sections. The Galerie du Roi, the King's Gallery, and the Galerie de la Reine, the Queen's Gallery, which is the longer one.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And a smaller side passage called the Galerie des Princes, the Princes' Gallery.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Who's in them now?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Chocolate shops, leather goods, a bookshop, a theatre, and a cinema.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Royal Theatre of the Galleries opened in the King's Gallery on the seventh of June 1847, just before the arcade itself.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And a cinema, the Cinéma des Galeries, opened in the Queen's Gallery in 1939.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And chocolate. I'm counting on chocolate.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: You'll find it. One of the best known names here is Neuhaus.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Tradition credits a Neuhaus, a Brussels chocolatier, with inventing the praline, the filled chocolate, in the early twentieth century.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The shop is right here in the gallery.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: I'm sorry, the praline was invented here?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: According to tradition. As with the Manneken Pis, I'd call it a good story with some truth in it.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But the shop is real, and I think it's worth a visit.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the cafés?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Taverne du Passage, in the Queen's Gallery, was called the Café des Arts until 1892, and it was a meeting place for writers and artists.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's still a restaurant, with a classic Belgian menu.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And film history.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: On the first of March, 1896, the Lumière brothers' films were shown to the public in Brussels in these galleries, just a few months after their first public screening in Paris.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So this is where Brussels first saw the movies.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In a glass-roofed passage. It's a lovely thought.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And the galleries were listed as a historic monument in 1986, and they're on UNESCO's tentative list for World Heritage.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Tell me one thing to look for.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Look up at the roof, then look down at the pavement.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The architect designed the whole thing as one piece, from the cast-iron frame to the shop fronts.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's a rare place where a nineteenth-century dream is still working.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And I'm told there's a little girl around here.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Yes. Back on the Rue des Bouchers there's a narrow alley called the Impasse de la Fidélité, the dead end of Fidelity, and at the end of it is a tiny bronze figure of a squatting girl, about fifty centimeters tall.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The Manneken Pis's sister.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Jeanneke Pis, installed in 1987.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Behind a little grille, so she's often hard to see.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: A bit of equality.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In a way. Pause here, have a coffee, buy some chocolate.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: When you're ready, we're heading toward a very grand building and the story of a vanished river.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Leave the galleries and walk west, toward the wide boulevard.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: You'll see the building long before you reach it.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It looks like a small palace.
